decisions.title: Batch rejected 4 proposals
decisions.body: claude (delegated by owner) completed one atomic batch. Outcomes: effect-cl-14-co-cognition-ac97054c0052: rejected; effect-cl-14-cognitive-drift-b108cccb20b8: rejected; effect-cl-14-constraint-collapse-5b6700ea9b63: rejected; effect-cl-14-memory-drift-7e627a94664c: rejected. No authoritative artifact was changed. Shared reason: DOMAIN_CONTAMINATION, delegated by owner. All four claims come from one source, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.33000278.v1 — a self-published Figshare collection titled Cognition in Mediated Systems: AI Memory, External Thought, Decision Fatigue, and Co-Cognition. The owner held Memory Drift pending one question: does the source study human memory or machine systems? It studies machine systems. The term comes from the collection paper Persistent AI Memory and the Extended Architecture of Human Thought, which concerns long-context AI, persistent memory stores and AI assistants; the proposal boundary says so itself — occurs within mediated systems involving AI and external cognitive tools — and its fact names the subject as systems that participate in memory and reasoning. That is not a claim about a person. The rejection is source-level, so all four go together rather than one at a time. Recorded honestly: of the four, constraint-collapse does have a human subject and a product-relevant variable (weakening defaults transfers coordination work onto individuals). It falls here anyway because its source is the same non-peer-reviewed essay collection, which the pipeline graded A at confidence 0.95 and which measured nothing. A defaults claim worth keeping should re-enter from a source that measured one. How the DOI passed relevance selection, two answers. First, recordRelevanceTier is a bag-of-tokens gate: CL-14 evidence_terms tokenise to cognitive, load, working, memory, extraneous, split, attention, information, processing; the title supplies memory and the abstract supplies four more, which scores tier 1 — the top tier, ranked ahead of genuine cognitive-load papers. The gate never asks who the study is about. Second and blunter, the run manifest for github-actions-30818192427 records records_skipped_irrelevant 0 against records_processed 293: the gate rejected nothing at all on that run, as on 19 of the 20 runs in run_history. The relevance pre-filter is not currently filtering.

decisions.title: Delegation protocol: transferability by rule, evidence fidelity by sampled human judgement
decisions.body: Splits the review burden by what each half actually requires. TRANSFERABILITY — whether a grounded claim names anything a product surface can act on — is judged BY RULE at extraction (D-160), because it reads only the claim and needs no source text, no expertise and no context; a human reading 210 pending proposals to answer it is a human doing arithmetic. EVIDENCE FIDELITY — whether the source is worth believing, whether the grade matches the design, whether a self-published essay collection has been treated as a study — stays a human judgement, because it requires reading the source and knowing what a claim of that shape usually costs. It is SAMPLED rather than exhaustive: the owner reads a sample deep enough to detect a systematic fault, not every record. DELEGATED VERDICTS are marked as such. A verdict decided by an agent on the owners instruction carries decided_by: "claude (delegated by owner)" and states its reason, and enters the audit sample exactly like any other decision — no exemption, no separate tier of trust. The first ten are D-149 through D-158. One code change follows from this and is part of the entry. lib/proposals.ts opened every decision body with the literal "Owner ${decidedBy}", which was true of every decision ever recorded until one was delegated. A log that calls a delegate the owner destroys the single fact the field exists to carry, so the literal is gone and the decider now names itself. What this does NOT delegate: nothing here lets a rule or an agent decide what is TRUE. Rule 8 is unchanged. Transferability judges usefulness, never validity, and a claim it refuses is held rather than contradicted.

decisions.title: Transferability filter at extraction, failing open
decisions.body: A deterministic pass in lib/transferability.ts, run in tools/extract.ts after strong grounding and before a grounded candidate can become an actionable proposal. It reads the CLAIM ONLY — fact, boundary, source title — never the source text, which is what makes it free to run and replayable offline from the proposal file alone. No model call: a rule that asks a model whether a claim is transferable reintroduces the judgement it exists to replace and could not be re-derived years later. FOUR CHECKS, each answering with a reason string whatever it decides. (a) SUBJECT, three-valued: a person interacting with an artifact passes; a person inside a specific institutional setting (classroom, clinic, programme, professional workflow) warns; neither a person nor an artifact — the subject is a system, a framework or a construct — refuses, because neither of the two admissible answers applies. (b) VARIABLE: does the claim name something an interface can change, matched against seven lexicons — layout, sequence, timing, wording, visibility, feedback, modality. (c) DIRECTION: does it state a direction, or only describe, define, or place something on a causal path. (d) POPULATION: does it depend on domain expertise the general product user does not have. SCORING as the owner specified it: failing (b) or (c) refuses; failing (a) outright refuses; a lone (a)-institutional or (d) warning does not — a classroom finding about layout may still transfer. ONE RULE THE OWNER DID NOT SPECIFY, named here so it can be overruled: the two warnings TOGETHER refuse, on the reading that "alone" implies the pair is more than a warning. It is recorded per verdict as escalated_by_warning_pair and measured separately, so its contribution is a number rather than a belief. Against the ten CL-14 verdicts it is worth exactly one row: 10/10 agreement with it, 9/10 without. FAILS OPEN, stated against the relevance skip by name. That gate merges record ids into skipped_irrelevant_record_ids, which the planner treats as terminal — a record removed from consideration with no diagnostic and no way back. Transferability does none of that. A refused candidate is WRITTEN to proposals/{type}/{id}.json with status held_non_transferable, hold_reason not_transferable, and the full verdict including all four reasons. It writes no reader coverage, marks no source record read, and deletes nothing. It is kept out of the actionable queue and out of the merge-target set, shown in /review under the held bucket with its four reasons, and one owner action puts it back in play. The verdict is stamped ruleset_version 1 and re-derivable by npm run replay-transferability; tools/validate.ts re-runs every stored verdict on every validation, so drift between the stored reasoning and the current rules fails the build rather than accumulating quietly. SCOPED TO EFFECTS. An L2 effect is a claim about people that the product layer must translate, which is where transferability is decidable. A realization already describes a shipped interface, and a mechanism or dossier is a container rather than a claim; judging those would produce confident verdicts about the wrong question. MEASURED, NOT TUNED. tools/transferability.test.ts holds the owners CL-14 verdicts as a frozen table, prints the agreement rate and every disagreement, and asserts determinism and completeness — never agreement, so no future lexicon edit can be justified by making the test pass. Two honest limits on the 10/10: the ruleset was written with the verdicts already known, so that number measures fit and not skill, and the real test is the queue nobody has judged yet. And on attention tunneling the rules reached the owners verdict by the wrong route — refused on SUBJECT while VARIABLE passed on the word "visual" inside "visual behavior", an outcome rather than a lever. It is left standing rather than patched: changing a lexicon after seeing the answer is the tuning this entry exists to prevent, and any future change bumps ruleset_version and gets its own decision.

decisions.title: The relevance pre-filter is not filtering
decisions.body: Exposed by the Memory Drift contamination rejected in D-158, and larger than it. recordRelevanceTier in tools/extract.ts scores a record by counting mechanism evidence_terms in its title and abstract. For CL-14 those tokenise to cognitive, load, working, memory, extraneous, split, attention, information, processing — so a self-published essay about persistent AI memory scored TIER 1, the top tier, ranked ahead of genuine cognitive-load papers. The gate counts words; it never asks who the study is about. The blunter fact is in the run history. The manifest entry for the run that produced these proposals records records_skipped_irrelevant 0 against records_processed 293, and 19 of the 20 runs in run_history report the same zero. The pre-filter is not narrowly admitting the wrong papers — on nearly every run it rejects nothing at all. Any reasoning that treats it as a working first gate is wrong, including the reasoning that a later filter is layering on top of one. Not fixed here, and deliberately so. The transferability pass (D-160) is the first gate of its kind in the pipeline and it is unproven on records nobody has judged; changing two filters at once would make neither measurable. Recorded as a standing defect: a mechanism-level gate that asks whose cognition a study measured is a separate piece of work, and it must fail open the way D-160 does rather than the way the relevance skip does.

decisions.title: Transferability VARIABLE becomes a model judgement (ruleset v2), v1 kept
decisions.body: Reverses one clause of D-160 — 'No model call' — for the VARIABLE check only, and records why the evidence forced it. SUBJECT, DIRECTION and POPULATION stay the deterministic rules they were; only VARIABLE changed, and it changed because a word list cannot cover the levers of eighteen mechanisms. WHAT THE PRE-IMPLEMENTATION EVALUATION SHOWED — ALL FIGURES IN THIS SECTION AND THE NEXT ARE ESTIMATES (D-131). They were produced outside this repository, before the code that would produce them existed, and NONE of them is reproducible from it: no committed script emits them, no artifact stores them, and no run has ever executed the path they describe. tools/transferability-report.ts, the only committed tool in this area, declares no LLM and no network and calls the v1 lexicon, so it cannot have produced any model figure below. Under D-131 these numbers motivate this decision; they do not authorize a commit against it, and the measured numbers that would must come from a run. WHAT IS MEASURED, and verifiable against the queue on disk: the denominators. 58 pending proposals across the six mechanisms furthest from CL-14 — SP-08 17, SC-06 9, ID-12 9, LA-01 10, ZE-07 4, CG-05 9 — out of 196 pending across 18 mechanisms. WHAT IS ESTIMATED: every numerator. The v1 VARIABLE lexicon, built from cognitive-load vocabulary, was evaluated as naming a lever for 1 of 58, with ten of eighteen mechanisms predicting zero transferable across the whole queue — the entire persuasion half the conversion funnel is built on — and the six VARIABLE passes it did produce read as lexical coincidence ('salience', 'cues', 'prompts', 'sequence') rather than comprehension: 'scarcity cues increase impulse buying' was refused as naming nothing an interface can change, when a countdown timer and a stock counter are interface elements. That example is inspectable and stands on its own; the counts around it do not. The reasoning holds — a word list cannot cover the levers of eighteen mechanisms — and it is the reasoning, not the arithmetic, that this decision rests on. THE NEW FORM. A cheap model pass reading only fact, boundary and source title, answering one question — does this name something a product surface can show, hide, reorder, count, time, or reword? It returns the lever it identified or states none exists, and the lever is stored on the VARIABLE check (identified_lever) so the reasoning is auditable and replayable offline. buildVariablePrompt in lib/transferability.ts holds the exact prompt, versioned in git next to the ruleset number. MODEL TIER IS PART OF THE DECISION, NOT A DETAIL — AND THE EVALUATED MODEL IS NOT THE CONFIGURED ONE. The evaluation criterion was right: 'do ten mechanisms still predict zero?', not agreement with owner verdicts, which measures fit and not skill. Its results are estimates. gpt-4o-mini was evaluated as naming a lever for 7 of the 58 and still predicting zero for LA-01 and CG-05 — reading an abstractly phrased 'X is a persuasion principle where…' as a definition and refusing it, a different false-refusal failure mode rather than a fix. gpt-4o was evaluated as naming a lever for 43 of 58 (SP-08 8/17, SC-06 8/9, ID-12 9/9, LA-01 8/10, ZE-07 4/4, CG-05 6/9) while still refusing the genuinely off-domain records — SARS-CoV-2 chemistry, CMMRD oncology, stock-market herding, medieval-literature analysis — i.e. discriminating rather than rubber-stamping. THE DISCREPANCY THAT MATTERS: gpt-4o is not reachable through any committed configuration. corpora/_ops/extraction.json configures the strong tier as anthropic/claude-sonnet-5, and judgeVariableViaModel resolves configuredTier(config, 'strong'), so a real run calls Sonnet. The routing decision — VARIABLE goes to the STRONG tier, via the existing OpenRouter setup (D-075) — stands, because it is a decision about CAPABILITY and the cheap tier's failure mode is the argument for it. What does not stand is the transfer of gpt-4o's numbers to the configured path: they are evidence about a model this pipeline does not call. The '$0.12 for 196 proposals' figure is likewise a gpt-4o price and does not correspond to configured strong-tier pricing; tools/transferability-probe.ts prints a measured cost at the configured prices, and a dry-run estimate before spending. On accounting: spend is counted against the per-run and monthly TOKEN limits in extraction.json, which are enforced live inside the call. corpora/_ops/budget.json holds caps only and has no spend section, so the earlier claim that the pass 'is counted against corpora/_ops/budget.json' overstated what that file records. HOW THE OFFLINE CONTRACT SURVIVES A NON-DETERMINISTIC CHECK. A model verdict cannot be recomputed offline the way a lexicon can, so replay changes shape rather than disappearing. lib/transferability.ts exposes replayTransferability(stored, claim): for v1 it recomputes all four checks and demands an exact match, unchanged; for v2 it AUDITS — it recomputes SUBJECT, DIRECTION and POPULATION deterministically and compares them exactly, structurally audits VARIABLE (pass or fail, a non-empty reason, a lever present exactly when it passed), and recomputes the scoring from the stored checks so a tampered verdict body cannot survive. tools/validate.ts calls replayTransferability on every stored verdict, so drift in the three rule-based checks and any incoherent verdict still fail the build; what it deliberately does not catch is the model changing its mind, which is a new judgement that only enters the store through a fresh extraction run stamping its own verdict. WHERE THE CALL LIVES. Only in the extraction path — judgeVariableViaModel in tools/extract.ts, reusing the OpenRouter client and budget accounting, run in GitHub Actions or an explicit dispatch, never in the app (rule 12). lib/transferability.ts stays free of network calls so validate, the report tool and the tests remain offline. It FAILS OPEN: a missing model id, a spent token cap, a transport error or a malformed answer yields no verdict, and the pipeline admits the claim to review without one rather than refusing it — a model outage must never silently bury a grounded claim. AMENDED by the decision that follows this one: admitting is still right, but the admission is now MARKED (verdict_unavailable, carrying the named reason) and COUNTED, because as first written an unjudged proposal was byte-identical to a judged one. V1 IS KEPT, NOT DELETED: judgeTransferability and its lexicons remain, old v1 verdicts still replay against them, and v1 remains the offline computation for the three checks v2 reuses. THE TWO REGRESSION FIXTURES (expertise-reversal-effect, dialogue-based-tts-lesson-format) stay red until a strong-tier run writes a stored v2 verdict that names their levers; the fixture reads the stored verdict rather than calling the judge, because the judge offline is v1 and would keep them red forever. gpt-4o named both in evaluation (expertise-conditioned guidance; speaker configuration), so a run should turn them green — and if a run ever refuses them, the stored verdict makes the false refusal visible again. D-161 still stands: the relevance pre-filter is left alone, so only one filter changes this round.

decisions.title: A fail-open admission is marked and counted (verdict_unavailable); silence is the defect, not the admission
decisions.body: AMENDS D-162's fail-open clause. Keeps the behaviour, ends the silence. THE DEFECT. D-162 made VARIABLE a model judgement and had it fail open — on a missing model id, a spent token cap, a transport error or a malformed answer, admit the claim without a verdict rather than refuse it. That direction is right and is not changed here: a model outage must never silently bury a grounded claim. What was wrong was the REPRESENTATION. judgeVariableViaModel returned a bare null on all five exits, and the caller expressed that as an ABSENT transferability field — which is also what a proposal written before D-160 looks like, and what a non-effect proposal looks like, since transferabilityClaimOfProposal returns null for every type but effect. Three distinct states, one representation, and no counter on any of them. An unjudged item was indistinguishable from a judged one. This is the same defect class as the 30-of-30 that stayed hidden for a month: not a wrong number, an ABSENT one, in a place where absence reads as success. THE FIX. judgeVariableViaModel returns a discriminated outcome carrying one of five named reasons — no_model_id, per_run_token_cap, monthly_token_cap, transport_error, malformed_answer. The caller stamps verdict_unavailable {ruleset_version, reason, detail?} onto the admitted proposal, increments ExtractionStats.verdict_unavailable and its per-reason split, warns on stdout per occurrence, and carries the totals into the manifest params, the run-progress summary, and the one-line run report — which previously printed neither this nor held_non_transferable, so the operator's summary of a run could not show that the filter had refused anything, let alone that it had never run. Five reasons rather than one boolean because a run that exhausted its token cap and a run whose model was unreachable produce the same total and demand opposite responses. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. It is NOT a CandidateFate. The candidate still receives its real fate — proposed, merged_into_pending, proposed_enrich — so the D-132 conservation equations are untouched and continue to balance. That is precisely why the separate counter is necessary: E1–E4 balancing is what made this loss invisible. Conservation proves no candidate vanished; it says nothing about whether anyone judged one. The extraction report prints the count adjacent to the conservation block and labelled as outside it. Validation is coherence-only: a proposal may not carry both a verdict and a reason there is none, may not record an unavailable verdict while not being a judgeable claim, and may not be held_non_transferable while recording that it was never judged. It is NOT required to carry either field, because all 211 judgeable proposals on disk carry neither — the pass has never run — and a gate demanding presence would fail the build on the existing queue while teaching nothing. Instead validate STATES the three-way split every run: judged, admitted unjudged, never touched. THE LAST OF THOSE IS THE NUMBER THAT MATTERED and had no reporting anywhere: today it is 211 of 211, and no verdict has ever been stored at any ruleset version. A filter that is enabled and has judged nothing looked exactly like a filter that judged everything favourably.

decisions.title: Probe spend is recorded in the extraction manifest, marked as a probe and exempt from the ledger
decisions.body: Reverses one clause of D-107 as it applied to the transferability probe: probe spend is now RECORDED in the extraction manifest. It keeps the other clause untouched — a probe still writes no candidate-ledger entry. THE DEFECT. tools/transferability-probe.ts spends real money on the strong tier and wrote its cost to stdout only, citing D-107's preflight precedent. That precedent covers a $0.0001 route-check. A probe over a mechanism's queue is ten strong-tier calls, and the monthly cap is computed by computeBudgetSnapshot -> computeMonthlyRollup, which sums run_history across committed manifests and reads NOTHING else. So every probe run was spend the cap could not see — the same failure mode D-099 fixed for runs that die mid-flight, arrived at from the other direction. Running the probe in Actions (so OPENROUTER_API_KEY never leaves the repo secret) makes it routine, which makes the invisible spend recurring rather than incidental. THE FIX. A `record-spend` flag, off by default and passed only by the workflow, appends ONE run_history entry: measured cost, dispatch_id from OPS_DISPATCH_ID, github_run_id, and the probe's own counts as params. last_run is deliberately not touched — lib/ops.ts loadExtractionRunSummary reads last_run to tell the showcase what extraction last did, and a probe overwriting it would report a measurement as a production pass. The entry is keyed by startedAt, so re-writing replaces rather than double-counts (D-099's identity). A probe that throws mid-loop records what it spent, then rethrows: the run fails with its accounting written. WHY THE ENTRY IS MARKED. params.mode = 'transferability_probe' (PROBE_RUN_MODE in tools/connectors/types.ts). D-132 makes tools/validate.ts require a balancing candidate-ledger entry for EVERY manifest run; a probe has no candidates, so it has nothing to balance. The two available moves were to write a zero-candidate ledger entry — fabricating the accounting the check exists to read — or to mark the entry and exempt it. Marked. The exemption is narrow and is itself checked: a probe entry that appears in the ledger, or that reports records_fetched or files_written above 0, FAILS validation, and validate prints how many runs the ledger check skipped so an unstated exemption cannot become an unread one. MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED (D-131). The workflow is workflow_dispatch only — no cron, no push trigger — and shares extraction's concurrency group, since both write the same manifest and spend the same cap. Its report goes to the job log and to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, so it is read without downloading an artifact. KNOWN COST, OWNER'S CALL. run_history is capped at RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT = 20 and all 20 entries are 2026-08, so a probe entry EVICTS the oldest run and that run's spend leaves the monthly rollup's view. The probe prints the evicted run's timestamp and cost rather than absorbing the loss silently. Raising the cap changes a contract shared with every connector manifest and was not made here.

decisions.title: Transferability ruleset v3: the named lever decides; SUBJECT, DIRECTION and POPULATION become recorded modifiers
decisions.body:
VARIABLE v2 works; the deterministic checks became the defect.

MEASURED BASIS. The first ruleset v2 probe over LA-01 (10 pending effect proposals, recorded in corpora/extraction/manifest.json) admitted 1 of 10. Reading the per-proposal output, the owner found that 8 of the 10 refusals were made by SUBJECT or DIRECTION on claims whose lever VARIABLE had already named. SUBJECT was refusing on where the study was run, not on whether the lever applies: anchoring refused for "public budgeting decisions", endowment for "rural villagers", herding for "salaried employees in India" — the lever in all three is an interface action. DIRECTION refused house money, hyperopic loss aversion and gain/loss framing, which are definitions whose direction is in the name. Only 2 refusals were correct — internet gaming disorder (a clinical trait with no interface surface) and overconfidence bias (a population correlation) — and BOTH were caught by VARIABLE returning "none identified", which is the check doing its job.

THE RULE. Ruleset v3: a named lever is the dominant signal. If VARIABLE identifies a lever, the claim is transferable. SUBJECT, DIRECTION and POPULATION still run, still state their reasons, and are recorded on the verdict as `modifiers_flagged` — confidence modifiers, never refusals. The only refusal path left is VARIABLE finding no lever an interface can act on. `escalated_by_warning_pair` is always false under v3: with no warning able to refuse, there is no escalation left to describe.

WHY MODIFIERS ARE STORED RATHER THAN DROPPED. The three checks were not deleted, because what they observe is true — a claim can be bound to a classroom and still carry a usable lever, and the owner should be able to see which ones were flagged when reading an admitted verdict. Deleting them would destroy the signal along with its misuse; recording them keeps the observation and removes only its power to refuse. This also keeps v3's SUBJECT/DIRECTION/POPULATION computation byte-identical to v2's (both call judgeDeterministicChecks), so the two rulesets differ in scoring alone and a v2 verdict can be compared with a v3 verdict on the same claim.

v1 AND v2 ARE KEPT. Same reasoning as D-162 kept v1: a stored verdict is only interpretable next to the rules that produced it. judgeTransferability (v1) and judgeTransferabilityV2 are untouched, and scoreChecksV3 is a separate function rather than a version branch inside scoreChecks — a shared function with a version flag would make two different rules look like one rule with an option.

SCOPE, STATED. This decision adds the v3 ruleset and a `ruleset=` option on the probe so v3 can be MEASURED. It does not wire v3 into tools/extract.ts, does not add an auditTransferabilityV3 replay path, and does not extend proposal.schema.json for modifiers_flagged. No v3 verdict is persisted onto any proposal by this change; the probe writes nothing to proposals/. Those are the steps that would follow an owner decision to adopt v3 in production, and they are deliberately not taken in advance of the measurement that would justify it (D-131: an estimate never authorizes a commit).

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX. The two documented false refusals pinned as regression fixtures (CL-14 expertise reversal, CL-14 dialogue-based TTS) are NOT resolved by v3. Both were refused by VARIABLE itself under the v1 word list — the one check v3 leaves sovereign — and neither proposal carries a stored verdict of any version (validate reports 0 of 211 judgeable claims verdicted). The fixture test reads the STORED verdict, and only a dispatched extraction run writes one; a probe cannot. So the fixtures stay red after v3, for a reason that is about where verdicts come from rather than about the scoring. Recorded here so the next reader does not mistake v3 for their fix.

decisions.title: Extraction manifest run_history and its candidate ledger are append-only; the 20-entry cap was silently undercounting the monthly spend cap
decisions.body:
THE DEFECT. tools/extract.ts's mergeExtractionRunHistory (RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT = 20) and tools/candidate-ledger.ts's mergeLedgerRuns (LEDGER_RUN_LIMIT = 20) both slice their history to the newest 20 entries on every write. The two are matched by design (candidate-ledger.ts's own comment: "matched to the manifest's run_history window so the two stay in step") because D-132 requires every non-probe run in run_history to have a balancing ledger entry. But the monthly spend cap (lib/status.ts computeMonthlyRollup) sums ONLY what run_history retains, and D-164's own text already named the mechanism without fixing it: "a probe entry EVICTS the oldest run and that run's spend leaves the monthly rollup's view... Raising the cap... was not made here." It surfaced concretely when the D-165 v3 probe over SP-08 evicted a $0.145989 / 275,177-token run — the probe printed the eviction, as designed, but nothing summed what a cap silently removes over time, so the safety-relevant number (this UTC month's spend against the USD/token cap) has been an undercount of unknown size since the first time run_history exceeded 20 entries.

THE AUDIT. Walked every commit in git history that touched corpora/extraction/manifest.json (29 commits) and diffed run_history between consecutive versions: any entry present in one commit and absent from the next, with no data-loss mechanism other than the cap, is an eviction. Found 28 evicted entries, totalling $0.7823 and 939,769 tokens. Nearly all (25 of 28) evicted within seven minutes on 2026-08-03, 10:37-10:44 UTC, during a wide CL-14 extraction — writeManifest persists a snapshot after every batch while a run is in flight (D-099), so one long-running extraction can burn through a 20-slot cap by itself. The most recent eviction was this decision's own trigger: the D-165 SP-08 v3 probe, 2026-08-06. Full list of evicted entries, with timestamps, targets and costs, is in this decision's supporting session log — not restated here since the constitution's context-discipline rule treats this as bulk data, not a fact to keep re-deriving.

THE FIX. Both merges are now genuinely append-only: replace an entry with the same identity (timestamp for run_history, run_id for the ledger — D-099's idempotency, unchanged), otherwise only ever prepend, never slice. tools/validate.ts's schema dropped run_history's `maxItems: RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT` accordingly — a shared upper bound could not be right for both an unbounded extraction manifest and every other still-capped connector manifest, so the schema now states only what is actually true of every manifest (at least one run) and leaves growth to each writer.

SCOPE, STATED. RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT itself (tools/connectors/types.ts) is UNCHANGED and still caps the SHARED connector manifest writer (tools/connectors/lib/manifest.ts), used by every corpus other than extraction — health checks, harvest jobs, and any future connector. That writer has the identical defect: computeMonthlyRollup reads its run_history too, so the monthly cap still undercounts whatever any of those connectors evicts. Not fixed here — it is a separate file, feeding a cap-correctness concern the same shape as this one, but without D-132's paired-ledger coupling to verify safe, and touching it was not what this decision was asked to do. Named so the next reader does not read this fix as closing the whole defect class.

ONE RECOVERED ENTRY, NOT RESTORED HISTORY. The ID-12 v3 probe (D-165, same dispatch batch as the SP-08 run that triggered this) measured real spend ($0.016348, 9 calls) that its own recordProbeSpend computed and printed, but never landed in the manifest — a concurrent job's commit won the race and its push was rejected. That figure is a MEASUREMENT, not an estimate (D-131 governs estimates; this already happened), so it was appended directly from the run's own log output once the append-only fix was in place — not re-run, since re-spending $0.016 to re-measure $0.016 already known would not be a fix. The 28 historically evicted entries from the audit above are NOT restored into run_history: doing so would change past UTC months' rollup totals retroactively, which is a different, larger decision than recording one already-measured, never-lost run, and was left for the owner rather than made here.

decisions.title: The effect anchor is not a citable record: its id is withheld from the prompt and citing it is its own named refusal
decisions.body:
MEASURED BASIS. Run 31092507605 (mode=realizations, effect=chromatic-asymmetry-in-visual-attention) read 406 of 427 eligible records, produced 25 candidates and 0 proposals. Of the 19 persisted refusals, 15 were unknown_record_id with the same detail: the model cited 'chromatic-asymmetry-in-visual-attention' — the anchoring EFFECT's id — in the record_id slot. This was not a corpus gap: the effect's own source record cr_255962234b8c859afa51401c was among the 406 records read, confirmed in coverage.json under by_effect. The model had the real source in front of it and cited the anchor instead. A second run on tracing-and-pointing reproduced it, 12 of 21.

THE CAUSE. anchorBlock serialised the effect as {id, name, fact, boundary, grade} into the same prompt where provenanceInstruction demands 'citations [{record_id,...}] using only supplied records'. The anchor was shaped exactly like a supplied record and carried the one field that makes a record citable. It is also the most quotable text in the context — it states the conclusion in a single sentence — so it is the path of least resistance for any model asked to ground a claim about that conclusion.

THE FIX, in three parts. (1) anchorBlock drops the id and introduces the anchor as 'THE CLAIM YOU ARE EXTENDING — NOT A SOURCE', stating there that it has no record_id and must never appear in citations. Nothing downstream needed the id in the prompt: effect_refs is written server-side in toProposal from the scope's own basis. This is D-104's rule applied one level up — a model-authored link to an artifact is provenance the model does not get to write, so it is not offered the handle. (2) The prohibition is repeated in provenanceInstruction, next to the citation demand it qualifies, because a rule stated only in a distant block is a rule read at the wrong moment. (3) groundingOutcome gains options.anchorEffectId and checks it BEFORE the record-map lookup, refusing with a new named reason anchor_cited_as_record.

WHY A SEPARATE REASON RATHER THAN unknown_record_id. The two look identical to a map lookup and have entirely different fixes: unknown_record_id means the model invented or misremembered an id, anchor_cited_as_record means it treated the claim it was asked to extend as the evidence for extending it. One counter for both is what let this hide — the run reported 15 unknown_record_id and read as a hallucination problem. Counted separately, the next run can say which failure is happening and whether the prompt change worked. Added to UNGROUNDED_DROP_REASONS and the three schemas validate.ts checks for drift; no counter or ledger work, because the reason maps are keyed dynamically and E1-E4 sum over fates, not reasons.

STRUCTURAL, NOT ADVISORY. The id is absent from the prompt entirely, so citing it is not something the model can be tempted into — the same reasoning as the synthesis projection, which strips quotes and record ids rather than asking for them to be omitted. The test asserts the absence, not the instruction: an instruction with no subject to act on cannot be disobeyed.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM. That yield returns. 3 of run 31092507605's refusals were proposal_not_built from the strong pass with empty citations, and 1 was premise_contradicted_downstream — a correct refusal of a claim the source itself later reverses. Only a re-run measures whether removing the anchor id converts the 15 into grounded candidates or merely redistributes them into other refusals. That re-run is one slice, and its result is reported with the two reasons counted separately.

decisions.title: Extraction spend is committed before validation and printed unconditionally; 'broken' becomes a reachable status and the synthesis fold check is gated on the fold count
decisions.body:
THE LOSS. Run 31095467232 (mode=realizations, effect=tracing-and-pointing) called OpenRouter, read 406 records, produced 27 candidates and 0 proposals, and committed NOTHING. Its spend is unrecoverable. Because the monthly cap is derived from committed manifests, August 2026's recorded spend understates actual spend by an unknown amount. This entry is that record.

THREE DEFECTS COMPOUNDED. (1) tools/validate.ts hard-failed on any checkLedgerBalance violation while separately REQUIRING an unbalanced run to be labelled 'broken' — so the only state satisfying the second check was one the first had already rejected. D-132's broken status existed in the type and in 0 of 22 committed runs; it was unreachable by construction. (2) extract.yml gated BOTH commit paths on the same npm run validate: the main commit ran after it, and the D-099 failure fallback re-ran the identical command and died the same way. (3) The fallback's error message said 'the run's spend is visible in the Actions log only'. It was not. tools/extract.ts had three console.log calls in 4816 lines and the terminal one printed stats — records, candidates, drops — with no tokens, calls or USD. Cost was computed into manifest.json and the ops-progress heartbeat and nowhere else. The message was a promise the code did not keep, which is worse than no message: it told the next reader to look somewhere the number had never been.

THE TRIGGERING VIOLATION WAS ITSELF WRONG. checkLedgerBalance refused a run where consolidated and expanded were both non-zero, calling it 'one absorbing the other's error'. recordSynthesisFold increments one side or the other per synthesis call, and both are run-level SUMS over every call, so a run where one mechanism folds 4 -> 1 and another folds 1 -> 3 sets both while E3 (into_synthesis + expanded == consolidated + candidates_strong) balances exactly. The slice-continuation driver makes multi-fold runs the norm. The check was a heuristic layered on top of conservation and was wrong at run level independently of the run that exposed it.

GATED, NOT DELETED. The ledger now records `folds`, and the check applies only when folds <= 1, where the statement is true and worth keeping: one fold cannot both consolidate and expand, so if it ever does, the fold arithmetic has been broken by an edit. Runs recorded before this entry carry no fold count and are not judged — asserting they folded once would invent a measurement nobody took. Deleting the check outright was rejected: it would have been indistinguishable from tuning a check to match a verdict it had just returned against us.

THE ORDER IS THE FIX. 'Is the money recorded' is now answered before 'was the run sound'. extract.yml commits corpora/extraction on always(), before validation; validation runs next; proposals commit only on success and stay fail-closed (rule 8); and a final always() step fails the job when this run's manifest entry says broken. A broken run therefore lands its accounting AND goes red. validate.ts reports rather than fails for a run its own manifest calls broken — the concession is to the admission, never to the imbalance; an unbalanced run not labelled broken still fails hard. The ledger's success line now prints 'N of M runs balance' so a broken run is never folded into a balanced count.

SPEND IS PRINTED BEFORE ANYTHING CAN BLOCK IT. reportMeasuredSpend writes calls, tokens in/out and USD to stdout on every terminal path — completion, run failure, and all-batches-failed — guarded so a run reports one spend. The Actions log is now the fallback the old error message claimed it already was.

WHY 31095467232 IS NOT RECONSTRUCTED. Its funnel numbers survive in the Actions log (27 candidates, 19 cheap / 8 strong, 21 dropped ungrounded: unknown_record_id 12, quote_not_in_source 1, proposal_not_built 8), but its cost does not. No committed code can query OpenRouter for historical spend: the only URL in the repo is /api/v1/chat/completions, cost is derived locally from each response's usage block times the price table, and generation ids are never persisted. Writing a manifest entry would require inventing a cost block, which D-131 forbids — a number not produced by the code that measures it is an estimate, and an estimate written into corpora/extraction would corrupt the one input the monthly cap trusts. The spend is recorded here as unrecoverable, with its reason, rather than recorded falsely.

decisions.title: The rejected-candidate corpus is append-only: the 20-file cap was destroying refusal evidence and could not even delete the file it claimed to
decisions.body:
THE DEFECT. tools/rejected-candidates.ts carried REJECTED_FILE_LIMIT = 20 and a pruneOldFiles that rmSync'd past it, with no logging, no return value and force: true (which also swallows ENOENT). It was called as a tail-call of flush(), which persistAccounting invokes after EVERY batch — so the deletion was not a maintenance pass, it ran mid-run, repeatedly.

MEASURED LOSS. Two files, 6 refusal records, both confirmed prune-caused by the 20 -> 21 -> prune -> 20 signature in their commits: 2026-07-31T10-09-59.574Z.json (3 x unknown_record_id, deleted by fead9ca, an LA-01 effects run) and 2026-08-03T10-37-43.467Z.json (3 x quote_not_in_source, deleted by 36ee483, this cycle's own chromatic-asymmetry run). The directory sat at exactly 20 when this was found, so the next refusing run would have destroyed another.

IT COULD NOT DO WHAT IT CLAIMED. The function sorted by mtime, with a comment asserting that mtime tracks the run and that filename sorting is unreliable across run-id shapes. Both are backwards. git checkout resets mtime, so the 20 committed files carried only 3 distinct mtimes for 20 distinct runs; with ties, sort order falls back to readdirSync order, so in CI the prune deleted an ARBITRARY file, not the oldest. Meanwhile fileNameFor emits exactly one shape — a zero-padded ISO-8601 timestamp — which sorts lexicographically and exactly. The rejected approach was the correct one. A further bug: `if (entry.name === keep) continue` skipped rather than compensating, so the directory could hold 21.

THE JUSTIFICATION HAD EXPIRED. The cap's only written basis was 'keep the committed history bounded the same way run_history is (20 runs)'. D-166 made run_history append-only — it already holds 22 entries — leaving the rejected directory the only capped side of a pair explicitly designed to stay in step. D-166's own scope note warned that its fix did not close the whole defect class and named RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT in tools/connectors/types.ts as another member; REJECTED_FILE_LIMIT was a third, uncaught because the audit was scoped to the manifest. No decision in the log ever authorised it: all 166 were searched.

THE MODULE CONTRADICTED ITSELF. Its header says it exists because 'the evidence for a fix evaporated with the Actions log', and promises 'Replay any file offline, forever'. pruneOldFiles sat 40 lines below that sentence, reintroducing precisely the evaporation the module was written to end.

THE LIVE RISK IT CREATED. tools/extraction-report.ts chooses its span_role source by comparing rejected-file rows against ledger totals, so a deletion silently shrinks the 'span_role refusals N of M' denominator and can flip the table's source. Measured at the time of the fix: rejectedRows = 40 against ledger dropReasons = 44, so the report was reading the ledger and the two deletions had changed no printed number. That was a coincidence of the twin D-166 defect — both deleted runs had ALSO been evicted from run_history — not a safeguard. With run_history now unbounded, every future prune would have deleted a file whose run was still in history. Margin before the source flipped: 4 records.

THE FIX. pruneOldFiles and REJECTED_FILE_LIMIT are deleted; flush() removes nothing. D-166's counter-argument against restoring history — that it retroactively changes past months' rollup totals — does not apply here, because rejection files are diagnostic only and feed no artifact (rule 8), so uncapping is purely additive. Archive-instead-of-delete was considered and rejected: it is a second mechanism to get wrong, and the repo-size concern the old comment raised is not yet real at 20 files and 59 records. If it becomes real, the answer is compression or a documented archive, stated in the module.

AND THE MODULE GETS A TEST. It had none — extract.test.ts imported only the pure rejectionRecord builder — which is how a destructive cap lived 40 lines under a promise of permanence without anyone reading the two together. tools/rejected-candidates.test.ts now asserts that flushing, repeatedly, removes no existing file, and it is wired into CI. The old cap's own value is the assertion's floor, so reintroducing a bound of 20 fails loudly.

decisions.title: A zero-yield run still consumes an effect's entire reader coverage: logged as a defect, deliberately not fixed in this cycle
decisions.body:
OBSERVED, not designed for. Run 31092507605 (mode=realizations, effect=chromatic-asymmetry-in-visual-attention) read 406 of 427 records, produced 25 candidates and ZERO proposals — every one lost to the anchor-citation defect fixed in D-167. Its coverage delta was committed anyway. Quoting the same slice afterwards returns eligible_total 427, already_completed 427, selected 0, 0 calls, $0. The effect cannot be re-read against a repaired prompt without mutating corpora/extraction/coverage.json, which would destroy the committed record of what was read — the exact accounting D-140 exists to keep honest.

THE COST, CONCRETE. The one slice the owner named to measure D-167's repair could not be used to measure it. tracing-and-pointing was substituted, and only because run 31095467232's commit failed entirely (D-168), so ITS coverage was never recorded. A defect saved the measurement from another defect; that is luck, not a property of the system.

WHY IT IS ONLY LOGGED. The right rule is genuinely unclear and deserves its own review rather than being decided inside a cycle scoped to three other fixes. Coverage means 'a reader was spent on this record', and that is TRUE even when the candidate died at the grounding gate — the tokens were paid and the model did read it. Re-reading the same record against the same effect with a repaired prompt is nevertheless a different question, which is the same argument D-140 made for keying coverage by effect in the first place. The distinction that probably matters is whether the run failed for a reason INTERNAL to the pipeline (a prompt defect, a broken gate) or external to it (the record genuinely says nothing usable), and the current code cannot tell those apart.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT. Either coverage becomes conditional on a candidate surviving to a proposal, or a run whose ledger records zero proposals rolls its coverage delta back, or coverage gains a prompt/ruleset version so a repaired prompt re-opens what an older one closed. The third is closest to how transferability verdicts already carry ruleset_version, and is the option to design first. None of them is attempted here.

STATED SO IT IS NOT REDISCOVERED. Anyone who sees a $0 quote on an effect with 427 eligible records should read this entry rather than conclude the corpus is exhausted.

decisions.title: The inferred realizations schema forbade the one field D-115 requires; prompt and wire schema are now checked against each other
decisions.body:
THE CONTRADICTION. inferredRealizationInstruction told the model to write {snake_case_name} in `pattern` rather than a bare number, and to declare each placeholder in `parameters`. The realizations/inferred branch of extractionItemSchema declared only id, term, description_as_reported, pattern, source_domain, artifact_context, and strictObject sets additionalProperties:false with every declared key required. Under response_format=json_schema the model therefore COULD NOT emit `parameters`. patternParameters returned [], patternParameterErrors found an undeclared placeholder, and toProposal refused the item as proposal_not_built. Every correctly-behaved answer was guaranteed to be rejected.

MEASURED COST. Three effect-anchored realizations runs, 88 candidates, ZERO proposals. Run 31092507605: 7 proposal_not_built. Run 31095467232: 8. Run 31104524768 (after D-167 removed the anchor-citation defect and grounding improved from 6 to 27 candidates entering synthesis): all 4 surviving strong candidates died here, each carrying params:null and a pattern declaring {tracing_mode}, {inactivity_threshold} or {trace_completions}. The single approved realization, expertise-based-guidance-toggle, has parameters only because the owner hand-edited it under D-118/D-119 — no run has ever produced one.

THE FIX. `parameters` is added to the inferred branch as an array of {name, value, unit}, matching what patternParameters actually reads. `unit` is included because :2887 silently drops any entry without one, which would have left yield unchanged for a new reason. The nested array-of-objects shape is not novel: citationsSchema ships it on every extract call and mechanismSynthesisSchema ships five of them on the strong tier.

TWO FIELDS REMOVED RATHER THAN RECONCILED. `evidence_basis` is dropped from the PROMPT instead of added to the schema. D-115 already says why: it is one literal, code-filled at extraction, never read from the model, because letting a model write it would let a model claim its own guess was measured. Asking for it was off-decision noise that also put the prompt out of step with the wire. `id` is dropped from the inferred SCHEMA: strictObject made it required while the inferred prompt never named it, and a model-authored id is discarded downstream anyway — the id is derived from the term, after a run labelled two different patterns "p1". Same rule as effect_refs and as the anchor id in D-167: do not ask for what nobody reads.

THE REAL FIX IS THE TEST. This defect was invisible because nothing compared the prompt with the schema — two artifacts describing the same contract, edited independently, never checked against each other. The new test parses the field list out of every prompt and asserts each name exists in the schema, across all 14 (mode, stage, derivation) combinations. Direction is prompt -> schema only: that is the direction that is impossible to obey, since additionalProperties:false makes the pipeline refuse compliance and then drop the candidate for the absence it caused. The reverse — schema requires a field the prompt does not name — is weaker, because strict mode makes the model emit it regardless.

THE TEST HAD TO BE WRITTEN FIRST AND SEEN TO FAIL. It reported exactly two rows — realizations/extract/inferred and realizations/synthesize/inferred, both demanding `parameters` — and nothing else, before the schema changed. A prompt-schema test that passed against the broken schema would have proved only that it was not looking.

PARSING IS DELIBERATELY STRICT, NOT LOOSE. The prompts carry three field-list conventions plus several lists that are VALUES, not fields: provenanceInstruction emits five span_role bullets into the same string as the real bullet list, the mechanism and dossier extract prompts enumerate section= names, and the dossier synthesis list names its five score axes. A loose match would absorb the mismatch it exists to find. The bullet parser is scoped to the block after "Fields per item:"; the semicolon parser is bounded to a single line so trailing HARD RULE prose is not read as fields; the comma parser stops at the first sentence end, because the synthesize variants append instructions after the list and would otherwise invent fields called "carry" and "remove". A row whose list cannot be parsed fails rather than passing silently — that assertion is the one that keeps the test honest as the prompts change.

itemSchema in the test suite gained a `derivation` argument. That it lacked one is the whole story: the inferred shape had never been schema-tested in any test, which is how an unsatisfiable schema survived three runs and a documented zero-yield diagnosis.

decisions.title: The extraction quote runs 5-6x high, and the dominant term is a pricing-selection bug that has been silently shrinking every run
decisions.body:
MEASURED. quoted vs actual, same scope, same committed price table: chromatic-asymmetry-in-visual-attention $1.0309 vs $0.17042 (6.05x); tracing-and-pointing $1.0290 vs $0.20311 (5.07x). The direction and magnitude are consistent. Note the quote is NOT stored per run — quote.json is gitignored and overwritten by every invocation — so these pair operator-recorded quotes with manifest actuals, and a run whose quote was not written down cannot be reconciled at all.

THE DOMINANT TERM IS NOT A COUNT. buildQuote prices every estimated input token at Math.max(cheap.input_usd_per_token, strong.input_usd_per_token) — the strong rate, 8x the cheap one — against a reality where 97-99% of input goes to the cheap tier (302,249 cheap vs 9,408 strong on the tracing run; 315,269 vs 3,861 on chromatic). The price TABLE is shared with the actual path; the selection of the RATE is not. Pricing the same estimate per tier gives $0.3335 instead of $1.0232 — roughly 84% of the overshoot, in one Math.max.

Decomposed for the tracing run: input $0.788246 quoted vs $0.094378 actual (8.35x); cheap output $0.135 vs $0.011037 (12.23x); strong output $0.100 vs $0.097690 (1.02x).

SECONDARY TERMS. output_reserved is not a prediction: it is 6000 per cheap call + 10000 per strong call, a flat function of call count, reserved as the API max_tokens. 100,000 reserved against 17,127 produced; cheap calls emitted 433 tokens against a 6,000 reserve. The char/4 input heuristic is close to right — 394,123 estimated vs 311,657 actual, 1.26x — and is not the problem. The quote models ONE slice with one strong call per mechanism, while the D-090 continuation driver ran 17 cheap + 2 strong; so the estimator simultaneously over-counts dollars 5x and under-counts calls.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS NOT THE ONE WE ASSUMED. An earlier report of this session said enforce=true would refuse a run whose quote exceeds per_run_tokens. That is wrong, and the truth is worse. The per-run cap is enforced by TRUNCATION (D-103): the planner appends records until the next would cross 500,000, then stops. That is why every quote landed at ~494k, 98.8% of the cap — the estimator is pressed flush against the ceiling by construction. A 5x-high estimator therefore truncated the slice to 375 records when roughly a thousand would have fit at true cost. It has been shrinking the corpus every run reads, not merely threatening to refuse one.

It does skew the gates that DO refuse: the monthly USD cap is reached after ~97 quoted runs instead of ~500 real ones, while the monthly CALLS gate is under-counted (16 quoted vs 19 actual) and so fires late.

NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY. The owner scoped this cycle to the four extraction fixes and named the estimator as the next thing after the pack. The correction is one line, but that line moves the truncation point, the monthly USD gate and the per-run cap together, so it changes how much corpus every future run reads. It needs its own measurement rather than riding along with a fix whose yield is being measured at the same time. Recorded now so the numbers above are not re-derived.

decisions.title: The D-168 accounting step discarded a SUCCESSFUL run's proposals: a fail-closed guard inherited an always() condition
decisions.body:
MY REGRESSION, introduced by D-168 and caught one run later. The old D-099 fallback ran only when the main commit had not succeeded, and inside it `git checkout -- proposals && git clean -fd proposals` was correct: it discarded a failed run's partial proposals so they could never reach the queue (rule 8). D-168 moved that block into a step that runs on `always()` and left the discard unconditional. On a SUCCESSFUL run it therefore deleted the proposals the run had just written, before the commit step downstream could add them.

MEASURED. Run 31107545446 (mode=realizations, effect=tracing-and-pointing, 12 remaining records): manifest records files_written 5 and held_low_confidence 5, and the commit contains only corpora/extraction. Five proposals were written and destroyed. They are not recoverable: the runner is gone, and the run consumed the last 12 records of that effect's reader coverage, so the slice cannot be re-read to regenerate them (D-170).

WHY IT SURVIVED ITS FIRST RUN. Run 31104524768 exercised the same step on the same day and showed nothing, because that run's files_written was 0 — every candidate died at proposal_not_built. A destructive step is invisible while there is nothing to destroy. The first run that produced output was the run that lost it.

THE FIX. The extract step gains `id: extract`, and the discard is gated on `steps.extract.outcome != 'success'`. Fail-closed behaviour is unchanged for the case it was written for; a successful run keeps its proposals for the validation-gated commit that follows.

THE LESSON, which is the reason this is a decision and not just a commit. A guard written for a failure path acquired an `always()` condition during a refactor and silently became a guard on every path. The condition moved; the reasoning in the comment above it did not, and still read as though it only applied to failures. When a step's `if:` changes, every conditional assumption inside its body is part of the change.

decisions.title: The quote prices each tier's own tokens, and the output estimate is separated from the max_tokens ceiling: one CL-14 slice now holds the whole relevant corpus
decisions.body:
TWO DEFECTS, ONE LINE APART. (1) buildQuote priced every estimated input token at Math.max(cheap.input_usd_per_token, strong.input_usd_per_token) — the strong rate, 8x the cheap one — though 92% of the estimate and 97-99% of measured reality is cheap-tier input. The output terms were already per-tier; only input collapsed. The form also re-derived 'the dearer tier' from the price table at runtime, so it would have flipped silently had cheap ever become dearer per input token. (2) CHEAP_OUTPUT_RESERVE = 6000 served as BOTH the API max_tokens ceiling and the output term in the truncation estimate. Measured cheap output is 433 tokens/call (7,358 over 17, run 31104524768) and 264 (run 31092507605), so a flat 6,000 per call reserved 20.2% of the per-run cap against tokens no run has produced.

THE FIX. estimateSelected keeps two input accumulators instead of one — the terms were always computed by separate expressions and merely summed into a shared variable — and ExtractionQuote.tokens carries input_cheap / input_strong / output_reserved_cheap / output_reserved_strong alongside the existing totals. buildQuote multiplies each by its own tier's rate. No weighting heuristic: the split is exact. This matters beyond accuracy, because transferability_probe runs are 0% cheap / 100% strong — a '97% cheap' constant would have been wrong for them, a per-tier calculation is right for both. CHEAP_OUTPUT_EXPECTED = 1500 is introduced for estimation only, a 3.5x margin over the highest measurement and 4x below the ceiling; CHEAP_OUTPUT_RESERVE stays 6000 and now appears at exactly one call site, the API request. Lowering the ceiling was rejected: it would truncate a response mid-JSON.

MEASURED, same 406-record selection, committed prices. Old formula $1.07086. Pricing fixed alone: $0.39986 (2.68x). Reserve fixed alone: $0.95611 (1.12x). Both: $0.28511 (3.76x). Against the three CL-14 realizations runs that have committed actuals, the quote goes from 5.07-6.05x high to 1.40-1.67x high — still conservative, which is correct for a gate.

THE CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS. Truncation compares tokens.total_upper_bound against per_run_tokens; it never reads dollars. Re-quoting the same 427-record CL-14 corpus: before, selected 375, remaining 31, capped TRUE, 494,123 tokens — 98.8% of the cap, pressed flush against the ceiling by construction. After: selected 406 (every relevant record; 21 are skipped as irrelevant), remaining 0, capped FALSE, 444,432 tokens. The whole relevant corpus now fits in ONE slice where it took two.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO D-172, WHICH OVERSTATED THIS. D-172 said a 5x-high estimator 'truncated the slice to 375 records when roughly a thousand would have fit'. Wrong twice. The 5x is the DOLLAR overshoot; the token overshoot was 1.50x, and only tokens drive truncation. And at 768-805 measured input tokens per record, 1,000 records would need ~965,000 input tokens against a 500,000 cap — the reachable figure was always 470-600, and the measurement landed at 406 relevant of 427 eligible, i.e. the corpus limit rather than the cap. The ~1,000 figure was 375 multiplied by the dollar ratio, which is not a quantity.

AND THE HARM WAS SMALLER THAN CLAIMED. Every mechanism corpus is under the corrected ceiling — CL-14 is the largest at 427 eligible, SC-17 next at 304 — and all three full CL-14 runs ended records_remaining 0, because the D-090 continuation driver read the truncated remainder in a second slice inside the same job. So the historical cost was wasted strong calls and a monthly USD gate firing after ~97 quoted runs instead of ~500 real ones. Not lost coverage. The fix is pre-emptive: CL-14 sits at 427 against a ~470 ceiling and the evidence connector keeps harvesting.

GUARDED BY TESTS THAT ASSERT THE ARITHMETIC, not the outcome: the quoted USD must equal the sum of per-tier (tokens x that tier's rate), and the old Math.max form must be strictly dearer than it, so a regression cannot pass; and CHEAP_OUTPUT_EXPECTED must differ from CHEAP_OUTPUT_RESERVE, sit below it, and keep margin over the highest measurement — so a later edit cannot re-fuse the ceiling and the estimate, which is the conflation that caused this.

NOT CHANGED: the reason strings. maturation.yml text-matches 'monthly (USD|token) cap' with jq to classify an exhausted budget as a pause rather than a block, so rewording them would break a consumer that no type checker can see.

decisions.title: LAYER 3 carries the transferred pattern and its parameters; the one screenshot-description realization is withdrawn
decisions.body:
THE PROJECTION BUG. realizationsFor in tools/render-packs.ts stopped at description_as_reported, dropping pattern, parameters, derivation and domain_transfer. The generator therefore received the SOURCE'S SENTENCE and nothing built from it — while the implementations section of the same pack shipped twenty hand-authored generation_directive entries with no DOI, no boundary and no transfer label at all.

THE ARGUMENT THAT SETTLED IT, from the owner, reversing his own earlier worry that a machine-written directive violated 'packs are evidence, not instructions': the pack's own `nature` line already says L3 preserves authored realization directives, and the implementations section proves directives already ship. A machine pattern carrying a corpus record id, a declared parameter with its unit and evidence_basis, and derivation=inferred is STRICTLY MORE HONEST than a hand-written directive carrying none of those. Dropping the fields was never a safeguard; it was a bug that made the less-evidenced artifact the only one visible.

WHAT IS EMITTED. All four fields are optional on the record and are spread conditionally, using the existing effect_id idiom, because a derivation='reported' realization declares none of them. This is not cosmetic: parseYaml reads `derivation: undefined` back as the STRING 'undefined', so the renderer's re-parse self-check would have passed a pack asserting a derivation nobody recorded. domain_transfer is a flow map, parameters a block sequence; every prose value goes through scalar(), which quotes only when YAML requires it — load-bearing for a pattern that opens with a {placeholder}, since a bare leading brace parses as a flow mapping.

THE VOICE CHECK MOVED WITH IT. voiceViolations exempted only the window between 'implementations:' and 'interactions:', leaving the realizations block scanned — harmless while L3 was description-only, and wrong the moment it carries a pattern, which is imperative by construction. The window now opens at 'realizations:'. Mechanisms, effects, boundaries and wiring stay scanned, which is the part that matters: a CLAIM written in the second person has stopped being evidence. No current pattern trips the check, so this was latent — but a check that fires on correct output is a check nobody reads.

AND THE MODULE BECAME TESTABLE. render-packs.ts called main() unconditionally, so importing it ran the renderer and wrote every pack — which is why realizationsFor had never been unit-tested, and how the dropped fields survived. It now guards on require.main === module, matching tools/extract.ts.

SEPARATELY, THE WITHDRAWAL. realizations/ZE-07/language-learning-landing-hero.json read 'The archived landing interface identifies Duolingo as a free language-learning product and names the supported languages' — a description of a page, naming no trigger, no interface change and nothing ZE-07 (open loops, goal gradient) is about. It carried no derivation, no pattern, no parameters, no domain_transfer and no effect_refs.

ROOT CAUSE, WHICH IS NOT THE EXTRACTION. tools/connectors/realization-wayback.ts fetches an archived page, strips tags, and accepts the result if it exceeds FORTY characters. The entire realization corpus is ONE record: rr_d6d2a2a98095047fc3acc42a, whose observation is 99 characters, because the 2015 Duolingo capture was JS-rendered and tag-stripping left essentially the <title>. The realization's quote is 82 of those 99. The manifest shows the prior run (capture=2026-07-01) FAILED that floor; the operator retried with capture=2015-01-01, which cleared it. A faithful realization derived from that record can only ever describe a page title, and both proposals do exactly that, honestly. The 40-character floor is the defect. It is reported here and NOT fixed — it needs its own measurement, and fixing it inside a pack-rendering change would bury it.

SCOPE OF THE PROBLEM, MEASURED. Of 13 realization proposals, 11 cite the evidence corpus and carry derivation=inferred. Exactly 2 cite the realization corpus, and both are this same record. So the shape is contained — but it is a 100% defect rate on a corpus of one, which argues the connector rather than the volume.

WHAT WAS DONE. The artifact is deleted and BOTH proposals set to rejected with the reason in decision_note (validate requires a non-empty note on rejection, so the reason lands in the data, not only here). Nothing referenced the artifact: effects/ZE-07/ does not exist, registry/mechanisms/ZE-07.json declares no effect_refs and none of its implementations carries realization_ids, so no reciprocal check is touched. Only owner approval creates an artifact, so only an owner reversal removes one — the 2026-07-24 approval stands in the log as what was believed then.

THE CORPUS RECORD IS KEPT. It is referenced by corpora/extraction/coverage.json and grounds the second proposal; deleting it would fail validate and rewrite what the connector actually fetched. The record is honest evidence of a thin harvest. The artifact built on it was the error.

ONE NEAR-MISS WORTH RECORDING. The second proposal carries a DIFFERENT payload id (duolingo-landing-page-hero), so validate's pendingRecordPaths duplicate-target warning would not have fired. Approving it would have created a second approved realization restating the same 99-character string, and nothing in the pipeline would have said so.

decisions.title: Ruleset v3 becomes the shipping transferability ruleset; the three steps D-165 withheld are taken
decisions.body:
Adopts ruleset v3 as the ruleset the extraction path applies, and takes the three steps D-165 named and withheld. D-165 withheld them for a stated reason — "deliberately not taken in advance of the measurement that would justify it (D-131: an estimate never authorizes a commit)" — so this entry exists to record that the measurement arrived and what it said.

MEASURED BASIS. A probe over every mechanism's pending queue, ruleset v2, the configured strong tier (anthropic/claude-sonnet-5), 195 calls, $0.382846, recorded in corpora/extraction/manifest.json under dispatch_id transfer-v2-wide. 196 proposals selected, 185 judged, 11 admitted without a verdict. Of the 185: 50 transferable (27%). VARIABLE NAMED A LEVER ON 185 OF 185 — it never once failed to find one. 105 of the 135 refusals (78%) were made against claims whose lever VARIABLE had already named. Refusals by check: DIRECTION 102, SUBJECT 79, VARIABLE 30. This is D-165's LA-01 reading at 18.5 times the sample, and it reproduces rather than contradicts it: LA-01 measured 1 of 10 again.

WHAT THE 30 VARIABLE REFUSALS WERE, because a filter that refuses nothing is not a filter. Medieval-literature rhetoric, molecular biology (FANCJ-mediated G4 resolution), cryptographic key generation from GPS, robotic motion planning, medical-imaging segmentation benchmarks, market-herding statistics, clinical epidemiology (CMMRD cancer incidence), neuroimaging analysis methods. VARIABLE is discriminating on domain, which is the job D-162 gave it. The two refusals D-165 called correct on LA-01 — internet gaming disorder, overconfidence bias — are both in this set again.

THE MEASURED EFFECT OF THE RULE CHANGE, scored offline from the same stored answers so the scoring change is isolated from the model's run-to-run variance: v2 50/185 (27%), v3 155/185 (84%), +105. Re-scoring those answers under v2 reproduces the run's own footer exactly (50/185, direction 102 / subject 79 / variable 30, 11 unjudged), which is what makes the v3 number a reading of the rule rather than of the parser. Per mechanism, every mechanism that admitted zero under both v1 and v2 recovers: ID-12 0 to 9/9, RE-10 0 to 6/6, SP-08 0 to 12/14, CG-05 0 to 7/9, EN-03 0 to 4/5. No mechanism admits zero under v3.

THE CHANGE, in three parts that must land together because any one alone fails validation. (a) tools/extract.ts calls judgeTransferabilityV3 and stamps verdict_unavailable with ruleset v3. (b) proposal.schema.json declares modifiers_flagged (array of subject|direction|population, not required, variable excluded by construction since the only check that can refuse can never be a modifier) — without it a stored v3 verdict fails npm run validate against additionalProperties:false, and validate is the step gating the proposals commit. (c) lib/transferability.ts gains auditTransferabilityV3, dispatched from replayTransferability — without it every stored v3 verdict returns "stored under unrecognised ruleset v3" and fails the build forever. The v2 and v3 audits now share auditSharedStructure, which is D-165's guarantee that the two rulesets differ in scoring alone expressed in code rather than in a comment.

v1 AND v2 ARE KEPT, unchanged, for the reason D-162 and D-165 both gave: a stored verdict is only interpretable next to the rules that produced it.

MEASURED, NOT TUNED. The frozen OWNER_VERDICTS table in tools/transferability.test.ts is untouched and still prints its agreement rate rather than asserting it. No lexicon was edited. v3 was adopted on a measurement of the queue, not on agreement with any past verdict.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, stated so the next reader does not overread it. It does not re-judge anything currently pending: the effects slice is exhausted for all 17 non-CL-14 mechanisms (already_completed equals eligible_total in every pre-flight quote), so extraction has no candidates left to judge and v3 governs future corpus additions only. The 196 pending proposals keep their absent-or-v2 verdicts. The two pinned regression fixtures stay red for the reason D-165 gave — both were refused by VARIABLE itself, the one check v3 leaves sovereign, and the fixture test reads a STORED verdict that only a dispatched extraction run writes. escalated_by_warning_pair is always false under v3 and the audit rejects a true one, since no scoring path can set it.

Second domain-contamination case after Memory Drift (D-158): both are the same failure mode — a keyword-only filter cannot tell a human-subjects study from an AI-systems study that happens to use the same vocabulary.

decisions.title: Every evidence record is abstract-only — methods, limitations, and effect sizes are structurally ungroundable
decisions.body:
Every evidence corpus record this pipeline has ever ingested is abstract-only. Measured directly against corpora/evidence/*.json (4,699 records, all 18 mechanisms): 0 carry full_text, 3,373 carry an abstract and nothing more, 1,326 carry no abstract at all (title/metadata only). This is not a sample or an estimate — it is every record on file.

Rule 12 is why: the whitelisted source connectors never return full text, so this is not a gap that will close as more sources are harvested — it is a structural property of what this pipeline is allowed to fetch. lib/source-context.ts's own header already states this for the single record it renders at a time ("the windowed 600-before/600-after branch is kept for a hypothetical future record type... today it is unreachable"); this entry states the corpus-wide consequence that follows from it.

THE CONSEQUENCE. Methods, limitations, and effect sizes live in a paper's body and results section — never in its abstract, which reports only the headline finding. So no fact this pipeline has ever extracted, and no fact it ever will while rule 12 stands, can be grounded in a study's methods, its stated limitations, or a reported effect size. Every extracted fact and boundary clause is grounded in what an abstract chose to summarize, not in what the underlying study actually did or how strongly it found it.

This is a different failure mode from the ones already on record. D-158/D-161's domain contamination is about a study measuring the wrong SUBJECT (an AI system dressed in human-cognition vocabulary). This is about every study, including a correctly-subject-matched one, being read through a single compressed paragraph that was never meant to carry grounding weight on its own. Grading (D-131 predecessor conventions) already discounts for source COUNT; nothing in the pipeline discounts for this — an A-band claim from one abstract and an A-band claim from a full paper's results section carry the same grade today, and only one of them could be checked against a stated effect size or limitation if it existed on file.

STATED AS A STANDING LIMIT, not fixed here. No connector change, no grading change, no schema change accompanies this entry. It exists so the next reader — extracting, grading, or reviewing a batch — knows this ceiling is structural before mistaking a well-graded abstract-only claim for one that was checked against a method or a number.

decisions.title: Proposal effect-ze-07-zeigarnik-effect-ff85288cec7e rejected
decisions.body: claude (delegated by owner) rejected effect proposal effect-ze-07-zeigarnik-effect-ff85288cec7e for ZE-07. No authoritative artifact was changed. Reason: NON_CONVERGENT_EVIDENCE — investigated per instruction before rejecting. 4 distinct DOIs are cited (5 provenance items), but they do not converge on the fact as stated. Only 1 (the 'Visual Zeigarnik Effect' paper) squarely supports the VISUAL-processing claim. 1 is about a different specific manifestation (anagram-solution recall, not visual paths). 1 is a general meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik/Ovsiankina effects, not visual-specific. 1 (cited via 2 quotes) is a methodological review whose own quote states the Zeigarnik effect is 'far from being the invariable result' and that 'more completed than incompleted tasks are recalled' in some studies — a source that CONTRADICTS the fact, already correctly used in the boundary field rather than in the fact itself. The mechanical cap rule (3+ independent sources -> B) assumes independent sources CORROBORATE the same claim; it has no way to detect that these four diverge, so applying it here would manufacture false confidence from a source count that does not mean what the rule assumes it means. No cap is reported for this proposal because none is honest.
